reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / WHO Classification of Endocrine Tumours
clinicalPearls: Now classified as oncocytic carcinoma of the thyroid, composed predominantly of large eosinophilic oncocytic (Hurthle) cells packed with abnormal mitochondria
Like follicular carcinoma, malignancy is defined by capsular or vascular invasion on histology, so aspiration typically returns an indeterminate oncocytic neoplasm result
Tends to occur in older patients and behaves somewhat more aggressively than conventional follicular carcinoma, with a greater tendency to nodal as well as distant spread
Frequently shows poor radioactive iodine avidity, so iodine-based treatment and imaging are less reliable than in other differentiated cancers
Characterised molecularly by widespread mitochondrial DNA mutations and chromosomal loss rather than the typical BRAF or RET drivers
Total thyroidectomy is the mainstay, with TSH suppression and thyroglobulin surveillance; radioactive iodine is used selectively given variable uptake
Functional imaging may be needed for restaging because non-iodine-avid recurrences can be missed on radioiodine scanning
reference.pathophysiology: Hurthle cell (oncocytic) carcinoma is a differentiated follicular-cell malignancy dominated by oncocytes, cells crowded with structurally and functionally abnormal mitochondria as a result of extensive mitochondrial DNA mutations and genome-wide chromosomal loss. As with follicular carcinoma, the diagnosis of malignancy depends on demonstrating capsular or vascular invasion rather than nuclear features. The oncocytic phenotype is associated with reduced expression of the sodium-iodide symporter, so many tumours concentrate iodine poorly, limiting the effectiveness of radioactive iodine and thyroglobulin-based radioiodine imaging and favouring earlier use of alternative functional imaging.
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic oncocytic tumour such as renal cell carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Neck ultrasound and ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration reported by the Bethesda system
Serum TSH and thyroid function to confirm euthyroidism
Serum thyroglobulin and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies for post-operative monitoring
Assessment of radioiodine avidity to guide use of radioactive iodine
Functional or cross-sectional imaging for non-iodine-avid or recurrent disease
Molecular profiling of indeterminate oncocytic aspirates where available
redFlags: Non-iodine-avid recurrence or metastasis undetectable on radioiodine imaging
Rapid growth, fixation, or hoarseness indicating invasive local disease
Bulky cervical nodal involvement or distant metastasis at presentation
Rising thyroglobulin with negative radioiodine scans suggesting dedifferentiated disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is favourable for small, minimally invasive, completely resected tumours but is worse than conventional follicular carcinoma when there is widespread invasion, nodal or distant spread, or poor iodine avidity limiting adjuvant options.
pitfalls: Relying on radioiodine imaging alone for surveillance when many oncocytic tumours are not iodine-avid
Attempting to diagnose malignancy on cytology, when only histological invasion distinguishes carcinoma from oncocytic adenoma
Underestimating the metastatic potential of these tumours compared with conventional follicular carcinoma
Overlooking oncocytic change in Hashimoto thyroiditis as a benign mimic on aspiration
references: WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
